'''Børge Christian Jessen''' (19 June 1907 – 20 March 1993) was a [[Denmark|Danish]] [[mathematician]] best known for his work in [[Mathematical analysis|analysis]], specifically on the [[Riemann zeta function]], and in [[geometry]], specifically on [[Hilbert's third problem]].

==Early years==
Jessen was born on 19 June 1907 in [[Copenhagen]] to Hans Jessen and Christine Jessen (née Larsen). He attended [[Skt. Jørgens Gymnasium]], where he was taught by the Hungarian mathematician [[Julius Pal]] during his first year.<ref name=Sparre>{{cite journal|last=Andersen|first=Erik Sparre|title=Børge Jessen: 19. juni 1907 - 20. marts 1993|journal=Det Kongelige Danske Videnskabernes Selskab: Oversigt over Selskabets Virksomhed 1993-1994|year=1993|pages=227–238|issn=0368-7201|language=da}}</ref> In 1925, Jessen graduated from the gymnasium and enrolled at the [[University of Copenhagen]]. During his time at the university he got to know [[Harald Bohr]],<ref name=E>{{cite journal |last1=Berg |first1= Christian|date=June 2009 |title=Børge Jessen, 19.6.1907 – 20.3.1993 |journal= Electronic Journal for History of Probability and Statistics|volume= 5|issue=1 |url=http://www.jehps.net/juin2009/Berg.pdf }}</ref> then a leading figure in Danish mathematics.<ref>{{cite book|last=Sørensen|first=Henrik Kragh|title=Viden uden grænser, 1920-1970|year=2006|publisher=Aarhus Universitetsforlag|location=Aarhus|isbn=8779341713|pages=105–124|editor1-last=Nielsen|editor1-first=Henry|editor2-last=Nielsen|editor2-first=Kristian Hvidtfelt|language=da|chapter=Matematik, statistik og datalogi|series=Dansk Naturvidenskabs Historie|volume=4}}</ref>  In 1928, Bohr established a collaboration with Jessen, which would last until Bohr's death in 1951.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ramskov|first=Kurt|title=The Danish Mathematical Society through 125 Years|journal=Historia Mathematica|date=August 2000|volume=27|issue=3|page=237|doi=10.1006/hmat.2000.2283|doi-access=free}}</ref>

After receiving his master's degree in the spring of 1929, Jessen embarked on a stay abroad. Supported by the [[Carlsberg Foundation]], he spent the fall of 1929 at the [[University of Szeged]], where he met [[Frigyes Riesz]], [[Alfréd Haar]], and [[Lipót Fejér]]. He then spent the winter semester of 1929–30 at the [[University of Göttingen]], where he attended lectures by [[David Hilbert]] and [[Edmund Landau]] while working on his [[PhD]] thesis. On 1 May 1930 Jessen defended his thesis in Copenhagen. He later elaborated the thesis into an article that was published in ''[[Acta Mathematica]]'' in 1934.<ref name=E /> The same year, he was appointed as a [[Docent#Northern Europe|docent]] at The Royal Veterinary and Agricultural University in Denmark.<ref>Olsen, L. W. (2003). ''Essays on Georg Rasch and his contributions to statistics''. Københavns Universitet, Økonomisk Institut. p. 23</ref>

In 1931,<ref name=Sparre /> Jessen married Ellen Pedersen (1903–1979), [[Cand.mag.|cand. mag.]] in mathematics and the daughter of [[Peder Oluf Pedersen]].<ref name=E /> Jessen continued to travel frequently in the early 1930s, visiting [[Paris]], [[Cambridge, England]], the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], [[Yale]] and [[Harvard University]] in America.

==Career==
Jessen was a professor of descriptive geometry at the [[Technical University of Denmark]] from 1935 till 1942, when he moved back to the [[University of Copenhagen]] where he was professor from 1942 to 1977 when he retired.  He was the president <!-- "formand for Carlsbergfondets direktion" may more correctly be translated to "chairman of the board"  /power.corrupts--> of the [[Carlsberg Foundation]] in 1955-1963<ref name=Pol>{{cite news |last=Fuglede |first=Bent |author-link=Bent Fuglede |title=Mindeord: Børge Jessens |newspaper=Politiken |location=Copenhagen |page=7 |language=da |date=26 March 1993 }}</ref> and one of the founders of the [[Hans Christian Ørsted Institute]].  He was the Secretary of the Interim Executive Committee of the [[International Mathematical Union]] (1950–1952), and in September 1951 he officially declared the founding of the Union, with its first [[Domicile (law)|domicile]] in Copenhagen.<ref>{{cite book|last=Lehto|first=Olli|title=Mathematics Without Borders: A History of the International Mathematical Union|year=1998|publisher=Springer|location=New York|isbn=0-387-98358-9|page=87|url=http://www.mathunion.org/fileadmin/ICM/Lehto/Lehto_Mathematics_Without_Borders/Lehto_Mathematics_Without_Borders.pdf}}</ref>  He was also active in the [[Danish Mathematical Society]].  After his death, the society named an award in his honor (Børge Jessen Diploma Award).
